title: Cup, cat and cot
what: merging /ʌ/, /æ/ and /ɑ/ or /ɒ/, so 'cup', 'cap' and 'cop' sound alike
summary: This subtle vowel distinction often goes unnoticed, as context usually clarifies meaning. However, merging these sounds can lead to ambiguity and requires listeners to exert more effort to understand. This can hinder clear communication in professional settings.
listenFor: Notice if the vowels in words like "cup," "cap," and "cop" are clearly differentiated in your own speech.

contrasts.wrong: He wore a blue cup to the game.
contrasts.right: He wore a blue cap to the game.
contrasts.note: The short 'a' in 'cap' is distinct from the 'u' in 'cup'.

contrasts.wrong: The baby slept in the new cut.
contrasts.right: The baby slept in the new cot.
contrasts.note: The 'o' in 'cot' is distinct from the 'u' in 'cut'.

contrasts.wrong: She gave the dog a gentle pot on the head.
contrasts.right: She gave the dog a gentle pat on the head.
contrasts.note: The 'a' in 'pat' is distinct from the 'o' in 'pot'.

contrasts.wrong: The dog's new collar was a vibrant collar.
contrasts.right: The dog's new collar was a vibrant color.
contrasts.note: The 'u' in 'color' is distinct from the 'a' in 'collar'.
